title: Welcome to the Designed World
heading: What happens when a useful machine breaks?
read: In Amy Smith’s grain-milling case, locate the part that wears out. Identify who has the tools to replace it.
question: A town needs a mill it can keep running. Which feature matters most after the first month?
correct: Parts the local operator can maintain
other: The highest speed on the first trial
reason: A fast first run tells you little about repairs. The screen matters because the operator needs a working mill over time.

title: Birth of a New Technology
heading: Two tests for the same fuel
read: Read printed pp. 12–14. Compare what happened when the sawdust mixture dried with what happened when it burned.
question: A fuel pellet holds its shape. What else must the team check before recommending it for cooking indoors?
correct: How much smoke it gives off in use
other: How fast they can make a larger batch
reason: The dried pellet passed a handling test. The smoke from burning it exposed a different problem for the user.

title: Designs That Take Flight
heading: Test one change at a time
read: Find an example of engineers using a model or test to improve a design. Identify what evidence could change the next version.
question: Which comparison tells you whether a single design change helped?
correct: Change one feature and repeat the original test
other: Change the shape, load, and test method together
reason: Changing several conditions hides the effect of the feature you want to evaluate.

title: Beyond Words
heading: Give the builder a usable view
read: Look at how Lam Loc represents a part. Compare an isometric view with flat views that show dimensions.
question: A teammate needs the depth of a hidden recess. What should you add?
correct: A dimensioned view showing the recess
other: A larger sketch of the same outside face
reason: Enlarging a face does not reveal hidden depth. A suitable view and a dimension let another person build it.

title: The Art of Engineering
heading: Design for a particular user
read: Find how an engineering team considers the person using a product. List a question the team could ask before choosing the shape.
question: Which interview question could change an organizer design?
correct: Which item is hardest to grab during your shift?
other: Do you like our finished organizer?
reason: An open question about the job exposes a need before the team settles on a solution.

title: Bringing Designed Ideas to the Market
heading: Ask the people doing the work
read: Find Araceli Ortiz’s market research example. Look for information that designers could miss when they assume what customers need.
question: What is the strongest check on a team’s assumption about its users?
correct: Observe a user doing the task and ask what gets in the way
other: Count the number of features in a competing product
reason: Feature counts tell you what is sold. Observing the job tells you whether those features solve a problem.

title: A Universe of Systems
heading: Follow the whole system
read: Find an input, a process, and an output in the manufacturing example. Trace one change beyond the station where it starts.
question: One station doubles its speed. What would show whether production improved?
correct: Count finished acceptable products over equal time
other: Time only the faster station
reason: A later station may still limit the line. Measure the output of the whole process.

title: The Making of a New Balance Shoe
heading: Test the fit during use
read: Find a decision where the shoe’s fit or performance matters to a user. Choose an action that would reveal poor fit in your own product.
question: An organizer holds every tool. How could it still fail its user?
correct: A user cannot retrieve a tool during the task
other: It has a different color from the original sketch
reason: Capacity alone misses access. Observe the user retrieving and replacing the real object.

title: Like Nature Intended
heading: Compare how a shape works
read: Find an example of a material or structure in nature that informs a design. Identify the useful feature and the job it does.
question: What would support borrowing a feature from a natural structure?
correct: A test showing it performs the needed function
other: A drawing that resembles the original shape
reason: Similar appearance is a starting point. Compare performance against the design requirement.

title: Redesigning America
heading: What changes when homes and shops share a site?
read: Read Peter Park’s account of urban sprawl and new urbanism. Find one decision that changes how a resident reaches a daily need. Mark the page.
question: Which plan gives a resident a realistic chance to walk to a shop?
correct: Homes and a shop connected by a short, usable walking route
other: Homes and a shop close on a map but separated by a barrier
reason: Short distance helps only when a usable route connects the two entrances. Trace a resident’s trip on the plan.

title: Bridging the Future
heading: Trace a load to the ground
read: In the Zakim Bridge case, follow a load from the deck through the supporting members. Separate a permanent load from a moving load.
question: Which is a live load on the bridge?
correct: A truck crossing the deck
other: The deck’s own weight
reason: The truck can move on and off. The deck’s own weight remains part of the dead load.

title: Tower in the Sky
heading: Use the first failure
read: Read about the tower’s response to forces. Look for a design decision that changes how the structure behaves under a sideways load.
question: A model leans at one joint before falling. What should you record first?
correct: Where and how the first change occurred
other: Only the final height of the collapsed pile
reason: The first change points to the weak part. The final pile alone can hide how failure began.

title: Home Sweet Home
heading: Sequence construction and inspection
read: Find a decision the construction manager makes before another crew can work. Identify a check that would be hard after an assembly is closed.
question: When should a team inspect a joint it will cover?
correct: Before the panel hides the joint
other: After the finished model is painted
reason: Checking while the joint is accessible makes a repair possible without dismantling the model.

title: From the Ground Up
heading: Match the material to the site
read: Read the geotechnical engineer’s account. Find one way conditions below a building change the design above it.
question: Which comparison helps decide whether two model foundations settle differently?
correct: Apply the same load to each and measure settlement
other: Use different loads and compare their final heights
reason: A common load makes the settlement comparison interpretable. Initial height and ground condition also matter.

title: Building Green
heading: Find a path for heat loss
read: Read Chris Benedict’s account of the building envelope. Trace a path through which energy can leave a heated space.
question: Which pair of trials can best show the effect of sealing a gap?
correct: Same enclosure and starting conditions, with and without the seal
other: A sealed large box compared with an open small cup
reason: Hold geometry, starting temperature, and test time steady to interpret the change.

title: A Race for the Sun
heading: Place a feature deliberately
read: Find a feature of the solar home that depends on where or how the house is built. Look for a design trade-off.
question: Which drawing best communicates a solar design choice?
correct: A labeled view showing the feature’s position and orientation
other: An unlabeled outline showing the area alone
reason: Position and orientation let a reviewer evaluate how the feature will interact with its surroundings.

title: In Deep
heading: Follow the pressure boundary
read: Find where the vehicle keeps people or equipment separated from the surrounding water. Trace the boundary in the illustration.
question: Why inspect a seal before testing a fluid device?
correct: A leak changes the pressure or flow the device can maintain
other: A leak changes only the outside appearance
reason: A leak creates another flow path. The device can lose the pressure difference needed for its job.

title: Shooting for the Moon
heading: Follow a fluid through a system
read: Look for a fluid-related design decision in the space mission. Draw an arrow to show the direction of motion or transfer.
question: A connected syringe moves less than expected. What should you check before changing its size?
correct: Air pockets and leaks at the connections
other: The color of the syringe barrel
reason: Compressible air and leaks can change the motion you observe even when the nominal syringe sizes match.

title: Fuel from the Fields
heading: Identify the input and the useful output
read: Find the fuel input and the useful motion in Joshua Tickell’s engine system. Draw an input-to-output path for a device at your bench.
question: Which observation measures useful output from a small press?
correct: How far it moves a load or changes a sample
other: How far the operator’s hand moves alone
reason: Hand travel is an input. Observe what the machine does to a load at its output.

title: An Ingenious Engine
heading: Turn heating into motion
read: Find how the design uses a temperature or pressure difference to produce motion. Compare the energy path with the boat’s engine diagram.
question: What must a heat-engine explanation include?
correct: How heating changes the working fluid and leads to motion
other: Only the direction the hull travels
reason: A direction describes the result. Trace heating, changes in the fluid, and the mechanical effect.

title: Energy from the Earth
heading: Compare heat source and output
read: Trace the geothermal source and the point where the system produces useful output. Mark one transfer on your own system diagram.
question: Why can the energy delivered as useful work be less than the heat supplied?
correct: Energy also transfers to the surroundings
other: The remaining energy disappears
reason: Energy can spread into the surroundings. Account for transfers when evaluating the system.

title: Good Chemistry
heading: Separate the energy source from the machinery
read: Find how heat from a reactor reaches a system that can produce electricity. Distinguish the fuel from the moving parts.
question: Which comparison is valid for two different heat engines?
correct: Trace the energy transfers in each system
other: Assume both use the same fuel
reason: Engines can use different heat sources while sharing steps that convert thermal energy to useful output.

title: Down the Pipes
heading: Compare two flow paths
read: Find a design decision involving flow through a pipe. Decide what would have to stay constant to test the effect of tube length.
question: What should stay the same when comparing two tube lengths?
correct: Tube bore and driving pressure
other: Time, diameter, and pressure can all vary freely
reason: Test one variable. A change in pressure or bore can change flow as well.

title: A Highway for Ideas
heading: Agree on a code
read: Find one rule that lets information travel between systems. Think about what a scoreboard operator and a receiver must share.
question: Two teams see the same on/off signals but read different digits. What should they compare?
correct: The order of the segments and the code key
other: Only the brightness of the lamps
reason: A receiver needs the same mapping and bit order as the sender. Equal brightness does not define the message.

title: Teaching a Machine to Listen
heading: Separate the signal from the trigger
read: Find a challenge in getting a machine to recognize speech. Decide what counts as a true response or a false alarm in a detector.
question: A detector sounds on every trial, including empty trials. Is that reliable detection?
correct: No, the device must distinguish a trigger from no trigger
other: Yes, making a sound every time is enough
reason: Test both conditions. A device that always responds cannot identify the event.

title: Shedding Light on Communications
heading: Follow information from end to end
read: Find how a message travels through an optical link. Identify what sends, carries, and receives the signal.
question: What would demonstrate that information crossed your link?
correct: A receiver correctly reports a message it could not see beforehand
other: The transmitter lights up when the sender presses a switch
reason: A working transmitter proves only one part of the system. Use a receiver and an unknown message.

title: Riding the Waves
heading: Choose the channel for the setting
read: Look for a communication design choice shaped by distance or the surroundings. Compare it with a cable or optical link.
question: Which question belongs in a communications plan?
correct: Will the signal reach the receiver through the actual environment?
other: Does the transmitter look like the receiver?
reason: The surroundings and distance affect whether a channel carries a usable signal.

title: Designed Learning
heading: Measure current in a branch
read: Find the model used to explain electric current. Trace one closed route before you place a meter.
question: How do you measure current through a lamp?
correct: Open its branch and insert the ammeter in series
other: Connect the ammeter directly across the battery
reason: Current in the branch must pass through the ammeter. A low-resistance current meter across a source can short it.

title: On the Grid
heading: Measure a difference between two points
read: Trace energy from source to user in the grid case. Mark the two points across which a component’s voltage is measured.
question: Where do the two voltmeter leads go to measure lamp voltage?
correct: At the two terminals of the lamp
other: Both at the same terminal of the lamp
reason: Voltage is a difference between two points. Touching the same terminal cannot measure the drop across the lamp.

title: Electrifying!
heading: Specify every operating state
read: Find how a building’s electrical system supplies and controls a load. Write an observable result for each switch position.
question: A fan runs at two speeds in one direction. Which requirement still needs testing?
correct: Reverse rotation under the specified control settings
other: Whether the battery holder has a label
reason: The workbook asks for speed control and reversal. Verify each operating state on the actual motor.

title: Sunny Side Up
heading: Budget energy when a source is intermittent
read: Find a solar design choice tied to the times power is available. Compare the supply period with the hours a lighthouse lamp must run.
question: Why include storage in a solar-powered lighthouse proposal?
correct: The lamp needs energy after sunset
other: Storage makes the lamp consume no energy
reason: Daily energy demand continues when sunlight is unavailable. Storage must cover the gap.

title: Cape Wind
heading: Defend a source against local constraints
read: Find a trade-off in developing a wind project. Compare supply, reliability, and site needs for the lighthouse.
question: Which argument best supports a power-source choice?
correct: A calculation of demand plus evidence about supply and storage at the site
other: The largest advertised peak power alone
reason: Peak power alone cannot show that the lamp will operate for its required hours.
